newsitem.title: USA: Nobel economics winner Vickrey keeps crusading.
newsitem.headline: Nobel economics winner Vickrey keeps crusading.

text.p: The U.S. winner of the 1996 Nobel Prize for Economics views his award as a soapbox.

"The opportunity to speak my piece and get it heard is much more important than the prize money," William Vickrey, professor emeritus of economics at Columbia University in New York, told reporters, students and colleagues.

Vickrey and British professor James Mirrlees won the prize, worth a total $1.12 million, for their separate contributions "to the economic theory of incentives under asymmetric information." The research of both focused on how organizations could make competent decisions based on incomplete -- or asymmetric -- information.
The Canadian-born Vickrey has spent his decades-long career crusading for innovative solutions to common economic problems of taxation, utilities and urban transportation.

His 1948 doctoral thesis, "Agenda for Progressive Taxation," proposed figuring taxes by adding up lifetime income and deducting past taxes. Such a system would eliminate capital gains tax confusion over when income was earned, Vickrey said.
His tax research rebutted earlier assumptions that differences in income should be neutralized by taxation. Instead, Vickrey observed that taxes negatively affect individuals' work incentive.

A common theme running through much of the economist's work is "congestion pricing," the notion that free market forces can influence consumers' use of roadways, airtraffic corridors, phone lines and other public thoroughfares.

In the 1950s Vickrey studied New York City transit prices, and in 1959 he proposed to Congress a solution for easing gridlock in Washington, D.C., with electronically assessed road user fees. The fees should rise gradually to peak at times of highest demand, thus discouraging congestion, Vickrey said.

The 82-year-old Nobel winner, who has been associated with Columbia University for more than 60 years, is trying to persuade people to cease "this insane pursuit of the Holy Grail of a balanced budget."
Deficit reduction imposes a dollar-for-dollar weakening of consumers' purchasing power, Vickrey cautioned in an unpublished paper he presented at the press conference.
"Ten billion dollars less of deficit means $10 billion less of disposable income ... and a loss of at least 100,000 jobs," the paper said.

Instead of striving for a balanced budget, politicians should seek a "balanced labor market" with unemployment far lower than the current 5.2 percent rate, Vickrey said. "We've just got to get politicians to understand macroeconomics a little better," he said.
Winning a Nobel Prize was gratifying, but not too much of a surprise. When he was told recently of his nomination, Vickrey figured his chances of winning were "50-50."
"It's not quite so much a surprise as being named president of the American Economics Association (in 1992)," he said.
The $1.12 million award was announced in Stockholm on Tuesday. Vickrey was telephoned by a member of the Nobel economics prize committee at about 5:45 a.m. (0945 GMT) on Tuesday morning, he said.

Vickrey was born in Victoria, British Columbia, in 1914 but moved to New York State when he was very young. He received his bachelor's degree in math from Yale University in 1935 and completed his graduate studies at Columbia.
He taught at Columbia beginning in 1946 and was named McVickar Professor of Political Economy in 1971.
